tasks.goal: A reader finds in docs/spec/ what rlsentry v3 is, its threat model, every area's scenarios for the next task, and this roadmap; documents only.

A user runs rlsentry on a folder of migrations or the lab and gets, per table, whether an anonymous visitor really read rows in a throwaway local copy, with evidence, as text and JSON; a live target is refused.

The same run also says, per table, whether an anonymous visitor really inserted, updated or deleted rows, including inserts a policy accepts only for chosen values; the whole lab shows every verdict kind.
Each run can also write one self-contained HTML report that opens offline and can be published as a Claude Artifact unchanged.
A user with Docker and no local PostgreSQL or PostgREST runs the same attack, with the copy in containers that are always removed.
A cited survey of related work (CVE-2025-48757 reports, existing Supabase and RLS scanners, research on access-control testing) says where rlsentry stands and what it does differently.
A user sees, per table and operation, whether one logged-in user could read or change another user's rows in the copy.
Views, storage buckets and database functions callable over the API are attacked as the anonymous visitor, with verdicts of their own.
An app the owner builds by hand the way an inexperienced user would, with the prompt recorded, becomes a lab target, and a write-up says what rlsentry finds in it.
A GitHub Action runs the attack on a pull request's migrations and fails the check when anything is exposed, attaching the HTML report.

A user who proves they own a live Supabase project, and opts in for the run, learns what an anonymous visitor could read or change there, without any write to real data and with no real value in the report.
